title: Traumatic Cataract: From Impact to Implantation
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the pathophysiology, classification, and complex surgical management of lens opacification resulting from ocular trauma. Essential for residents and fellows managing anterior segment emergencies.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Traumatic cataract is the opacification of the crystalline lens resulting from blunt or penetrating ocular injury. It is a leading cause of unilateral visual impairment in children and young adults. Pathogenesis involves direct mechanical rupture of the lens capsule, osmotic swelling of lens fibers, or metabolic disruption (in the case of radiation or electric shock).

rows: Petal-shaped opacities along posterior lens sutures
Imprinted iris pigment on the anterior lens capsule
Rapid hydration of the entire lens cortex
Absorption of lens proteins leaving collapsed capsule

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination
content: Visual Acuity: Assessment of light projection (PR) if cataract is mature.
Pupils: Check for RAPD (indicates optic nerve or severe retinal damage).
Slit-lamp: Assess capsule integrity, phacodonesis, and iridodonesis.
Gonioscopy: Look for angle recession, cyclodialysis, or IOFB in the angle.
Tonometry: Rule out phacolytic, phacomorphic, or traumatic glaucoma.
Fundoscopy: B-scan required if view of the posterior pole is obscured.

sections.title: Diagnostic & Imaging Workup
content: Step 1: B-scan Ultrasonography to rule out Retinal Detachment (RD) or Vitreous Hemorrhage.
Step 2: Non-Contrast CT Orbits (1mm cuts) for suspected Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB).
Step 3: UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy) for visualizing zonular loss or sulcus anatomy.
Step 4: Biometry (IOL Master/A-scan) using the fellow eye for comparison if necessary.

rows: Often bilateral, no history of trauma, stable
History of metal injury, ERG changes (decreased b-wave)

sections.title: Emergency Surgical Indications
content: Phacomorphic Glaucoma (Intractable IOP elevation from lens swelling)
Phacolytic/Lens Protein Uveitis (Uncontrolled inflammation)
Ruptured Lens Capsule with cortical material in the anterior chamber
Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB) requiring immediate removal
Total Lens Subluxation into the Vitreous Cavity or Anterior Chamber

sections.title: Surgical Management Strategy
content: 1. Preoperative Control: Stabilize inflammation with topical/systemic steroids.
2. Incision: Consider sclerocorneal or small-gauge pars plana lensectomy if zonules are <180° stable.
3. Capsulorhexis: Use trypan blue; manual or femtosecond laser (if stable) to visualize the capsule.
4. Lens Removal: Low-parameter phacoemulsification or manual ECCE to minimize zonular stress.
5. Vitrectomy: Perform anterior vitrectomy if vitreous prolapse is present.
6. IOL Selection: In-the-bag (with CTR), Sulcus (if capsule allows), or Scleral-Fixated (Yamane/Gore-Tex).

sections.title: Surgical Tools for Zonular Instability
content: Capsular Tension Ring (CTR): For <4 hours of zonular dialysis.
Cionni Modified CTR: Scleral suturing for >4 hours of dialysis.
Capsular Tension Segments (CTS): Ahmed segments for focal support.
Iris Hooks / Capsule Hooks: Temporary intraoperative support.
Trypan Blue Dye: Critical for identifying capsular tears.

content.explanation: T: Tension (Zonular loss/IOP); R: Rosette (Cataract morphology); A: Angle (Recession/Hyphema); U: Uveitis (Lens-induced); M: Mechanism (Blunt vs Penetrating); A: Adnexa (Lid/Canalicular involvement).

sections.title: Postoperative Complications
content: Secondary Glaucoma (Steroid-induced or Angle-recession)
Retinal Detachment (Highest risk in penetrating trauma)
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME)
IOL Decentration or Dislocation
Endophthalmitis (Especially if IOFB involved)
Sympathetic Ophthalmia (Rare but devastating bilat. uveitis)

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Amblyopia: Rapid visual rehabilitation is critical for patients <7 years old.
IOL Power: Tendency toward under-correction to account for axial growth.
Inflammation: Children exhibit a more robust inflammatory response (Corticosteroid burst required).
PCO: Primary posterior capsulotomy and anterior vitrectomy are standard in young children.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Recent Advances
content: Pearls: Always perform an indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression (if safe) to rule out peripheral retinal breaks.
Pearls: Avoid MRI if there is even a 1% suspicion of a metallic IOFB; use CT instead.
Advances: Flanged intrascleral IOL fixation (Yamane technique) provides excellent stability in the absence of capsular support.
Advances: Use of pupillary expansion devices (Malyugin ring) in cases of traumatic miosis or iris sphincter damage.
